title: Module 13 Challenge: A Correlation With a Decision Attached
scenario: A researcher gives 30 students a short scale of academic self-efficacy and records their course grades. The correlation is r = .41. The researcher uses alpha = .05, two-tailed. A second researcher with a sample of 12 students from another course finds r = .41 on the same measures. A department chair reads both and says, "One is significant and the other is not, so these studies disagree."

parts.q: For the study with n = 30, what is the decision?
o: Reject the null. The critical r for df = 28 is about .361
Retain the null because r is under .50
Reject the null because r squared is .41
Retain the null because n is small

parts.q: The second study (n = 12) has the same r. What is the critical r at df = 10, alpha = .05 two-tailed?
o: About .576, so r = .41 is not significant
About .80, so r = .41 is not significant
parts.why: With df = 10 the critical value is .576. The same r is not significant in the smaller sample.

parts.q: Respond to the chair. Explain why the two studies actually agree, what each result tells you about the size of the relationship, and what would give a more precise estimate.
parts.model: The two studies found the same correlation, r = .41, which accounts for about 17 percent of the variability in grades. The difference in significance arises only from sample size. With 30 students the critical r is .36, so .41 is significant. With 12 students the critical r is .58, so .41 is not. The estimates agree. The smaller study simply has too little precision to separate .41 from zero. A confidence interval for r in each study would show wide overlap. The best way to settle the question is to combine the information, for example with a larger sample or by pooling the two studies, which gives a more precise estimate of the true correlation.
check: I said the studies agree on the size of r
I attributed the difference in significance to sample size
I mentioned r squared or an interval to describe size or precision
I suggested more data or pooling
